metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization is the share of provisioned compute doing real work over time, and it is the denominator that makes every other efficiency claim about a data center honest.

The definition is narrow in a way that matters. It measures against provisioned capacity rather than installed capacity, so the figure reflects how much of what has been made available is actually used. It is also measured over time rather than at peak, which is the harder and less flattering choice. A fleet can look fully committed at its busiest hour and still waste most of its provisioned compute across the year.

This is a power metric as much as a financial one. Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing, and compute that is provisioned but unused still draws from the building. Utilization is therefore the point where capacity planning, capital spending, and electricity demand meet. Any provisioned compute figure is an upper bound, and utilization is what discounts it.

What the data does not give is a number. There is no target rate, no measured rate, no benchmark, and no stated method for deciding what counts as real work. It also does not say how utilization should be weighed against the physical constraints listed beside it, stranded power and space per cabinet and floor loading limits, which govern what a building can hold rather than what its servers are doing. This is a definition, and it should be read as one.
